text.p: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- UK RANKS SECOND FOR FOREIGN TAKEOVERS

A survey compiled by accountancy firm KPMG reveals that acquisitions of UK companies by foreign corporations in 1996 reached a record $38.54 billion (23 billion stg). The figure represents an 8 per cent increase on the previous year, and puts the UK second only to the US as a target for corporate acquisitions in a global league table. More than half of the acquisitions of UK companies involved US buyers, including six of the 10 biggest UK businesses sold overseas last year.
-- FORD SEEKS STATE AID FOR HALEWOOD

Ford, the automotive giant which last week announced the axing of 1,300 jobs at its Halewood plant on Merseyside, has revealed that it has approached the government for aid to ensure future production at the plant. The job losses will result from a decision to switch production of the company's new Escort model to Spain and Germany. However, Ford has said it met with trade secretary Ian Lang last week to discuss government aid, which could influence the company's plans on whether to go ahead with production of a new, unspecified, model at Halewood after 2000.
-- MILLENNIUM PROJECT IS BACK FROM THE BRINK

The controversial Greenwich millennium project is set to be confirmed by national heritage secretary Virginia Bottomley on Monday, after a week of extraordinary political wrangling. The Labour party had threatened to effectively veto the project unless it secured assurances over a review of costs and of potential government liability. The project will go ahead following an agreement reached on Friday night between the Labour party, the government, and the Millennium Commission.
-- LABOUR PUTS BUSINESS AT HEART OF CAMPAIGN

Tony Blair, leader of the opposition Labour party, has rebuffed newspaper claims that the party intends to raise 10 billion stg from its proposed windfall tax on the privatised utilities, and that the range of utilities subject to the levy is to be broadened. Blair, whose plans to put business policy at the heart of Labour's general election strategy are in danger of being undermined by the issue of the levy, refuted the suggested figure of 10 billion stg, and said that the details of the tax "will be for discussions in government".
-- BA AND PILOTS FORGE 'NEW WORKING RELATIONSHIP'

British Airways and the pilots' union Balpa have agreed to a 10-point set of principles detailing a new working relationship. The move follows industrial action by the union last summer, and is seen as taking both sides out of the trenches of confrontation and away from a dogmatic approach. The 10 principles cover areas such as exchange of information, flexibility and problem solving.
-- SALOMON FORGES ALLIANCE WITH BROKERAGE

US investment bank Salomon Brothers has formed a strategic alliance with Fidelity Investments, the US fund management and brokerage group, which could herald a new trend in the US financial services sector. Under the deal, Salomon is able to distribute some of the equities it underwrites through Fidelity's discount brokerage network. The arrangement fills a gap for both parties, and could be the first of a wave of strategic alliances in the sector, rather than the mergers and acquisitions prevalent at the moment.
-- ELF ACQUITAINE IN HUNT FOR SPECIALITY CHEMICALS DEALS

French oil, chemicals and pharmaceuticals group Elf Acquitaine has said it is seeking speciality chemicals acquisitions in a bid to strengthen its presence in Asia and the US. Although the majority of any future deals will be relatively small, designed to plug gaps in the company's portfolio, group chairman Philippe Jaffre has indicated that a large deal, worth up to 1.67 million stg, is also a possibility. In an interview, Jaffre also revealed that he was prepared for Elf's share in its quoted drugs arm Sanofi to sink to 'between 20 and 40 per cent' as part of a merger with another drugs group.
-- GM WOULD CONSIDER MORE DISPOSALS

General Motors, which last week announced an agreement to sell the defence operations of its subsidiary Hughes Electronics to Raytheon for $9.5bn, has said it would consider more disposals of non-automotive operations if the Hughes deal fails to lift the value of its shares. In an interview, GM chairman Jack Smith indicated that if another disposal were necessary, the telecommunications and satellite business of Hughes could be next to go.
-- VOLVO'S TRUCK DIVISION HIT BY AMERICAN SLUMP

Swedish vehicle maker Volvo has reported a 17 per cent decline in its deliveries of trucks in 1996, mainly due to a slump in sales in North and South America. North America in particular was badly hit, with deliveries falling by 38 per cent. In Europe, demand remained firm, with deliveries falling only marginally from 35,190 to 35,030 units. The company's US division Volvo GM - which is 13 per cent owned by GM - has reported an improvement in orders in December and January, and is expected to reach break-even by mid-year.
-- RUHRGAS WIDENS NETWORK OF SUPPLIERS

German gas company Ruhrgas has announced new contracts with gas suppliers in Norway and the Netherlands, as well as with BP of the UK, in a move to widen its network of long-term suppliers. Ruhrgas also signed a large long-term contract involving gas from Norway last summer, and in total the agreements are worth about 19 billion stg. The company has contracted to buy a total of 1,450 billion cubic metres of gas in the years ahead, covering all of Germany's gas import requirements until 2010.
